label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
# The house in Glenmore

Dear all,

I'm writing this once, for everyone, because I'd rather you heard it properly from me than in bits on the phone. Some of you already know part of it. This is all of it, including the parts I'd sooner leave out.

I have agreed to sell the house in Glenmore, the old Mulkerrin place where Tom grew up. The sale was agreed on the 3rd of November and it closes on the 15th of January. I'm putting the date here so nobody hears it from someone else again.

## How you found out

I'll start with the part I got wrong. Some of you heard about the sale before I had told you myself, and Declan heard it from his cousin Gráinne on a WhatsApp. That is my fault. I had been meaning to ring everyone properly and I was slow about it, and news in this family travels faster than I do. Declan found out in the worst way a person could, and I'm sorry for that. I'm sorry to Gráinne too, who was put in an awkward spot through no doing of her own, and to anyone else who felt they were the last to know.

I'm sorry for how you found out. I'm not sorry for the decision. I know those two can sound close together, and I'll try to explain the difference as I go.

## The house

For anyone who has never been, or was too young to remember, the house is near Oughterard, about forty minutes from me. Tom's grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin, built it in 1931. Tom grew up in it, and I spent a good part of my married life going in and out of that back door. When Tom died in March 2024, it became mine to look after, and I have looked after it. Every fortnight since, I've driven out, forty minutes each way, to open the windows and run the taps and check the pipes. I've told myself that was only what needed doing. It was also a way of keeping Tom close, and I know that.

Two years is a long time to keep a house going for the sake of keeping it going.

## Why

There are practical reasons and there is one that is harder to write, so I'll do the practical ones first.

In September I had the roof surveyed by Ó Flaithearta's. The slates need doing and so does the back chimney. The quote was €38,000. There's damp in the back bedroom as well. And the septic tank needs replacing, which would have to be done to sell to anyone at all. A house of that age that stands empty doesn't stay as it is. It goes the wrong way quietly, and I could see it going.

Now the harder reason. Last February I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get myself up. Nobody was passing, there's rarely anyone passing, and I remember thinking very clearly that nobody knew where I was. I got up in the end, and I told nobody. Not Úna, not anyone. You are reading it here for the first time, which is probably not the right way to tell you either, but I wasn't ready to say it out loud before now.

Since then I've been afraid of being alone in that house. I'm not afraid of ghosts. I'm afraid of ice and stone steps and being seventy-one with nobody coming. I can't go on maintaining the place on my own, and I won't ask any of you to take it on from three continents. I wouldn't be fair to you, and it wouldn't be fair to the house.

Over the best part of two years I've come to understand something I didn't expect to. I can keep Tom's memory without keeping the house. I used to think the two were the same thing, that if I let go of the one I'd lose the other. I don't think that anymore. Tom is in plenty of places that don't have a roof that needs €38,000 spent on it.

## Who is buying it

The buyers are a young couple, Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, so he knows the area and the weather. They have two small children, and they want to live in the house. It won't be a holiday let and it won't be sitting empty for eleven months of the year.

I should say that the price was fair, but it wasn't the highest I was offered. Over the summer a Dublin crowd offered more. I took the lower offer on purpose, because I knew what the Dublin crowd would do with it, and I didn't want that. I wanted it to be a house with a family in it again.

Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. He said it more than once, and he said it when he was well. I've thought about that a great deal. If I held on to the house the way I was holding on to it, I'd be turning it into exactly the thing he didn't want.

## What is being kept

Because I know that's what matters most to some of you, here is what's staying with the family:

- The dresser is going to Úna.
- Pádraig's fiddle.
- The photographs.
- The Sacred Heart lamp.
- The sign from the gate.

The Joyces have also said that family can come out and walk the land any time. They meant it, and they said it before I asked. I don't want anyone to feel that the door to the place is shut because the deeds are changing hands. You'll be walking up to a different front door, that's all.

## What I remember

I've been thinking about all the things that happened there, and here are some of them.

Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind that house in 1979. It was raining, as you'd expect, and the cattle were watching. I said yes mostly because I was drenched and wanted to go inside. That isn't quite true, but it's close enough to be family history.

Then there are the children learning to swim in the lake below the house. Declan wouldn't come out of the water until his lips were blue. I'd call and call, and he'd shout back that he was nearly finished, and I knew perfectly well he wasn't. I can still see him standing there, shivering and furious that anyone was suggesting he stop.

I'm not going to lose those. They didn't happen to the slates or the septic tank. They happened to us, and we're bringing them along.

## Declan

Declan, I know you read these, so this part is for you, though I hope the rest of the family will forgive me for saying it in front of them.

When you rang me in the middle of the night, you said I was selling your father. I understand why you said it. You'd just heard it from a cousin, in a message, with no warning, and I understand that it felt like the floor going. I said things back to you that I shouldn't have said. I won't repeat them here and I won't pretend I didn't say them.

I'm not angry with you. I want you to know that clearly. I think we were both hurt and both tired and neither of us was at our best at that hour.

I do regret not talking to you before it went any further. You should have been one of the first to hear, and I should have rung you myself. But I'll be honest with you, because I'd rather be honest than comfortable: I wasn't willing to wait until your summer visit to decide. Another winter of that step and that roof wasn't something I could face. I made the decision I needed to make. What I got wrong was the telling.

The door is open. It's open whenever you want to ring, at whatever hour suits you, and I'll pick up. If you want to shout at me, I'll listen to that too. And if you'd like to come and see the house once more before it goes, there's a day for it, and I'd like you to be there.

## The day out

Which brings me to the invitation. On Sunday 13th December, before the house is cleared, I'm opening it up for the family. Anyone who can come is very welcome. I'll have soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies, because the haggard hasn't improved, and the lake path will be wet.

I'd like it to be a day for walking through the rooms, telling the old stories, correcting each other's versions of them, and seeing the house once more with the family in it. Those of you in Boston and Perth and Leeds, I know it's a long way for a Sunday. If you can't be there, I'll take plenty of photographs, and I'll talk to every one of you after.

## Last thing

I've written a long post, and I don't think it's as neat as I'd like it to be. I'm not at peace with every part of it, and I don't expect all of you to be either. If you have questions, ask me. If you're annoyed, tell me. I would much rather hear it from you directly than learn about it from a cousin.

The sale closes on the 15th of January. Come on the 13th of December if you can.

---

I've left off a sign-off since you'll know how you'd usually close to this crowd. Check the spelling of the names and the Irish, in case I've got a fada wrong, and change anything that doesn't sound like you. The joke about saying yes because you were drenched is mine, so cut it if it isn't something you'd say. I also left out any specifics about what you said to Declan, since you didn't tell me.
